#| include: false
library(dplyr)
library(plotly)

set.seed(258)

plot_cols <- list(
  teal       = "#00695c",
  teal_dark  = "#004d40",
  teal_light = "#e0f2f1",
  blue       = "#c8e6f3",
  blue_soft  = "#eef8fb",
  grey       = "#f5f6f7",
  yellow     = "#fff8e1",
  orange     = "#f9a825",
  red        = "#c62828",
  text       = "#2f3437",
  muted      = "#667174",
  border     = "#d8dee2",
  code       = "#f3f4f5",
  white      = "#ffffff"
)

plotly_anova_layout <- function(
  p,
  title = NULL,
  x_title = NULL,
  y_title = NULL,
  height = 345,
  margin = list(l = 62, r = 20, t = 54, b = 58)
) {
  p |>
    layout(
      title = list(text = title, font = list(size = 16), x = 0.02),
      height = height,
      margin = margin,
      xaxis = list(
        title = x_title,
        zeroline = FALSE,
        showline = TRUE,
        fixedrange = TRUE,
        linecolor = plot_cols$border,
        gridcolor = "rgba(0,0,0,0.08)"
      ),
      yaxis = list(
        title = y_title,
        zeroline = FALSE,
        showline = TRUE,
        fixedrange = TRUE,
        linecolor = plot_cols$border,
        gridcolor = "rgba(0,0,0,0.08)"
      ),
      dragmode = FALSE,
      paper_bgcolor = "rgba(0,0,0,0)",
      plot_bgcolor = "white",
      showlegend = FALSE
    ) |>
    config(
      displayModeBar = FALSE,
      displaylogo = FALSE,
      scrollZoom = FALSE,
      doubleClick = FALSE,
      responsive = FALSE
    )
}

## Chapter Roadmap {.compact}

:::: {.three-col}
::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">8.1 - ANOVA idea</span>
Use one test to compare several population means.
:::

::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">8.2 - Variation split</span>
Separate total variation into treatment variation and error variation.
:::

::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">8.3 - F-test</span>
Build the ANOVA table and use a right-tailed F distribution.
:::
::::

<br>

:::: {.three-col}
::: {.stat-card .fragment}
<span class="label">8.4 - Assumptions</span>
Normal residuals, equal population variance, and independent observations.
:::

::: {.stat-card .fragment}
<span class="label">8.5 - Comparisons</span>
After a significant ANOVA, use Fisher's LSD or Bonferroni.
:::

::: {.stat-card .fragment}
<span class="label">8.6 - R workflow</span>
Use `oneway.test()`, `aov()`, and `pairwise.t.test()`.
:::
::::

---

## Why ANOVA?

::: {.defbox}
**Analysis of Variance**, or **ANOVA**, is used to compare several population means.

Suppose there are $k$ groups, usually with $k \ge 3$.
:::

:::: {.three-col}
::: {.stat-card .fragment}
<span class="label">Bad habit</span>
Run many separate two-sample tests.
:::

::: {.stat-card .fragment}
<span class="label">ANOVA habit</span>
Start with one global test:

$$H_0:\mu_1=\mu_2=\cdots=\mu_k$$
:::

::: {.stat-card .fragment}
<span class="label">Interpretation</span>
If the global test rejects, then at least one population mean differs.
:::
::::

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
ANOVA does **not** immediately tell us which mean is different. That comes later with pairwise comparisons.
:::

---

## One-Factor ANOVA Model

:::: {.two-col-wide}
::: {.col}
::: {.defbox}
The textbook model is:

$$
Y_{ij}=\mu+\tau_i+\epsilon_{ij},
\qquad
\epsilon_{ij}\sim N(0,\sigma^2)
$$

where $Y_{ij}$ is observation $j$ in group $i$.
:::

::: {.notebox .fragment}
<span class="label">Meaning of the pieces</span>

- $\mu$: overall mean
- $\tau_i$: treatment effect for group $i$
- $\epsilon_{ij}$: random error
- $\mu+\tau_i$: mean of group $i$
:::
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.defbox .fragment}
Equivalent form:

$$
Y_{ij}=\mu_i+\epsilon_{ij},
\qquad
\epsilon_{ij}\sim N(0,\sigma^2)
$$

where $\mu_i$ is the population mean of group $i$.
:::

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
Each observation in the same group is modeled as having the same population group mean, plus random error.
:::
:::
::::

---

## Data Structure and Notation

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.col}
| Group 1 | Group 2 | $\cdots$ | Group $k$ |
|---:|---:|:---:|---:|
| $X_{11}$ | $X_{21}$ | $\cdots$ | $X_{k1}$ |
| $X_{12}$ | $X_{22}$ | $\cdots$ | $X_{k2}$ |
| $\vdots$ | $\vdots$ | $\ddots$ | $\vdots$ |
| $X_{1n_1}$ | $X_{2n_2}$ | $\cdots$ | $X_{kn_k}$ |
| $\bar X_1$ | $\bar X_2$ | $\cdots$ | $\bar X_k$ |
| $S_1^2$ | $S_2^2$ | $\cdots$ | $S_k^2$ |
| $n_1$ | $n_2$ | $\cdots$ | $n_k$ |
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.notebox}
<span class="label">Notation</span>

- $\bar X_i$: sample mean of group $i$
- $S_i^2$: sample variance of group $i$
- $n_i$: sample size of group $i$
:::

::: {.defbox .fragment}
Total sample size:

$$n=n_1+n_2+\cdots+n_k$$

Overall sample mean:

$$
\bar X=
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{k}\sum_{j=1}^{n_i}X_{ij}
=
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{k}n_i\bar X_i
$$
:::
:::
::::

---

## Sources of Variation

::: {.defbox}
ANOVA works by splitting the total variation into two pieces.
:::

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.stat-card .fragment}
<span class="label">Within groups: error variation</span>

$$
SSE=\sum_{i=1}^{k}(n_i-1)S_i^2
$$

This measures residual variation inside the groups.
:::

::: {.stat-card .fragment}
<span class="label">Between groups: treatment variation</span>

$$
SSTr=\sum_{i=1}^{k}n_i(\bar X_i-\bar X)^2
$$

This measures how far group means are from the overall mean.
:::
::::

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
If group means are far apart compared with the within-group noise, the ANOVA F statistic becomes large.
:::

---

## Total Variation and Decomposition

:::: {.two-col-wide}
::: {.col}
::: {.defbox}
Total variation:

$$
SSTotal=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\sum_{j=1}^{n_i}(X_{ij}-\bar X)^2
$$
:::

::: {.notebox .fragment}
<span class="label">Decomposition identity</span>

$$
SSTotal=SSTr+SSE
$$
:::
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.thinkbox}
ANOVA asks whether the **between-group variation** is large relative to the **within-group variation**.
:::

::: {.examplebox .fragment}
If all group means are similar, $SSTr$ should be small.

If at least one group mean is far away, $SSTr$ gets larger.
:::
:::
::::

---

## The ANOVA Table

| Source | df | SS | MS | F-statistic |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Treatment | $k-1$ | $SSTr$ | $MSTr=\dfrac{SSTr}{k-1}$ | $F^*=\dfrac{MSTr}{MSE}$ |
| Error | $n-k$ | $SSE$ | $MSE=\dfrac{SSE}{n-k}$ |  |
| Total | $n-1$ | $SSTotal$ |  |  |

::: {.notebox .fragment}
<span class="label">Mean square rule</span>

$$
MS=\frac{SS}{df}
$$
:::

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
The F statistic compares treatment variation per degree of freedom with error variation per degree of freedom.
:::

---

## Hypothesis Test and Reference Distribution

:::: {.two-col-wide}
::: {.col}
::: {.defbox}
Hypotheses:

$$
H_0:\mu_1=\mu_2=\cdots=\mu_k
$$

$$
H_a:\text{at least one }\mu_j\text{ is different}
$$
:::

::: {.notebox .fragment}
<span class="label">Test statistic</span>

$$
F^*=\frac{MSTr}{MSE}
=
\frac{SSTr/(k-1)}{SSE/(n-k)}
$$

Under $H_0$:

$$
F^*\sim F_{k-1,n-k}
$$
:::
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.thinkbox}
The ANOVA p-value is always a **right-tail** probability.
:::

::: {.warnbox .fragment}
Large $F^*$ means the treatment variation is large compared with error variation.
:::
:::
::::

---

## ANOVA P-value Visual

:::: {.two-col-wide}
::: {.col}
::: {.notebox}
<span class="label">Example reference distribution</span>

For $k=3$ groups and $n=18$ observations:

$$
df_1=k-1=2,
\qquad
df_2=n-k=15
$$

The shaded region is the p-value:

$$
P(F_{2,15}\ge F^*)
$$
:::
:::

::: {.col}
```{r}
#| echo: false
x <- seq(0, 8, length.out = 500)
fstar <- 1.70

f_df <- data.frame(
  x = x,
  density = stats::df(x, df1 = 2, df2 = 15)
)

shade_df <- f_df |> filter(x >= fstar)

plot_ly() |>
  add_trace(
    data = f_df,
    x = ~x,
    y = ~density,
    type = "scatter",
    mode = "lines",
    line = list(color = plot_cols$text, width = 2.5),
    hovertemplate = "F = %{x:.2f}<br>Density = %{y:.3f}<extra></extra>"
  ) |>
  add_trace(
    data = shade_df,
    x = ~x,
    y = ~density,
    type = "scatter",
    mode = "lines",
    fill = "tozeroy",
    fillcolor = "rgba(249,168,37,0.35)",
    line = list(color = "rgba(249,168,37,0.85)", width = 1.5),
    hovertemplate = "Right-tail p-value<extra></extra>"
  ) |>
  layout(
    shapes = list(list(
      type = "line",
      x0 = fstar,
      x1 = fstar,
      y0 = 0,
      y1 = max(f_df$density) * 0.92,
      line = list(color = plot_cols$teal_dark, width = 2.4, dash = "dash")
    )),
    annotations = list(list(
      x = fstar + 0.55,
      y = max(f_df$density) * 0.55,
      text = "p-value",
      showarrow = FALSE,
      font = list(size = 13, color = plot_cols$text)
    ))
  ) |>
  plotly_anova_layout(
    title = "Right-tail p-value for ANOVA",
    x_title = "F",
    y_title = "Density",
    height = 345
  )
```
:::
::::

## Example: Margarine Container Fill Amounts

:::: {.example-grid style="display: grid; grid-template-columns: 0.88fr 1.12fr; grid-template-rows: auto auto; gap: 10px 18px; align-items: stretch;"}

::: {.taskbox style="grid-column: 1; grid-row: 1; font-size: 0.61em; line-height: 1.14; padding: 10px 14px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
A consumer group compares three margarine brands.

The values below are the amount above or below the advertised 500 ml label.

<br>

| Brand 1 | Brand 2 | Brand 3 |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 2 | 1 |
| 3 | 2 | 2 |
| 3 | 4 | 4 |
| 0 | 3 | 2 |
| 1 | 0 | 3 |
| 0 | 4 | 4 |

Summary:

| Brand | $\bar x_i$ | $s_i^2$ |
|---|---:|---:|
| 1 | 1.33 | 1.87 |
| 2 | 2.50 | 2.30 |
| 3 | 2.67 | 1.47 |
:::

::: {.stat-card style="grid-column: 2; grid-row: 1; font-size: 0.77em; line-height: 1.13; padding: 13px 17px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Calculation</span>

$$
\bar x=\frac{6(1.33)+6(2.50)+6(2.67)}{18}=2.17
$$

$$
SSE=(6-1)(1.87)+(6-1)(2.30)+(6-1)(1.47)=28.20
$$

$$
SSTr=6(1.33-2.17)^2+6(2.50-2.17)^2+6(2.67-2.17)^2=6.39
$$

$$
MSTr=\frac{6.39}{2}=3.20,
\qquad
MSE=\frac{28.20}{15}=1.88
$$

$$
F^*=\frac{3.20}{1.88}=1.70
$$
:::

::: {.notebox style="grid-column: 1; grid-row: 2; font-size: 0.61em; line-height: 1.13; padding: 10px 14px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">ANOVA table</span>

| Source | df | SS | MS | F |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Treatment | 2 | 6.39 | 3.20 | 1.70 |
| Error | 15 | 28.20 | 1.88 |  |
| Total | 17 | 34.59 |  |  |
:::

::: {.examplebox style="grid-column: 2; grid-row: 2; font-size: 0.64em; line-height: 1.14; padding: 11px 14px; margin-bottom: 0; display: flex; align-items: center;"}
With $df_1=2$ and $df_2=15$, $p\approx0.216$.

Since $p>0.05$, do not reject $H_0$. These data do not give strong evidence that the three brands have different mean fill differences from 500 ml.
:::

::::

## Example: Campus Café Pickup Systems

:::: {.example-grid style="display: grid; grid-template-columns: 0.88fr 1.12fr; grid-template-rows: auto auto; gap: 10px 18px; align-items: stretch;"}

::: {.taskbox style="grid-column: 1; grid-row: 1; font-size: 0.63em; line-height: 1.16; padding: 11px 15px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
A campus café wants to compare mean pickup wait time across three ordering systems.

The data are summarized by group.

<br>

| System | $n_i$ | $\bar x_i$ | $s_i^2$ |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Mobile order | 6 | 7.0 | 2.0 |
| Kiosk order | 6 | 8.5 | 2.8 |
| Counter order | 6 | 10.2 | 3.1 |

Use ANOVA at the 5% level.
:::

::: {.stat-card style="grid-column: 2; grid-row: 1; font-size: 0.77em; line-height: 1.13; padding: 13px 17px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Calculation</span>

$$
\bar x=\frac{6(7.0)+6(8.5)+6(10.2)}{18}=8.57
$$

$$
SSTr=6(7.0-8.57)^2+6(8.5-8.57)^2+6(10.2-8.57)^2=30.76
$$

$$
SSE=(5)(2.0)+(5)(2.8)+(5)(3.1)=39.50
$$

$$
MSTr=\frac{30.76}{2}=15.38,
\qquad
MSE=\frac{39.50}{15}=2.63
$$

$$
F^*=\frac{15.38}{2.63}=5.84
$$
:::

::: {.notebox style="grid-column: 1; grid-row: 2; font-size: 0.61em; line-height: 1.13; padding: 10px 14px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Hypotheses</span>

$$
H_0:\mu_1=\mu_2=\mu_3
$$

$$
H_a:\text{at least one system mean wait time differs}
$$
:::

::: {.examplebox style="grid-column: 2; grid-row: 2; font-size: 0.64em; line-height: 1.14; padding: 11px 14px; margin-bottom: 0; display: flex; align-items: center;"}
With $df_1=2$ and $df_2=15$, $p\approx0.013$.

Since $p<0.05$, reject $H_0$. There is evidence that not all ordering systems have the same population mean wait time.
:::

}

</style>

:::: {.two-col-wide style="grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr; gap: 18px; align-items: start;"}

::: {.col}
::: {.notebox style="font-size: 0.58em; line-height: 1.10; padding: 8px 11px; margin-bottom: 6px;"}
<span class="label">Margarine example</span>
:::

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
anova_summary <- function(n, xbar, s2) {
  k <- length(n)
  N <- sum(n)

  grand <- sum(n * xbar) / N
  SSTR <- sum(n * (xbar - grand)^2)
  SSE <- sum((n - 1) * s2)

  df1 <- k - 1
  df2 <- N - k

  MSTR <- SSTR / df1
  MSE <- SSE / df2
  Fstar <- MSTR / MSE
  pval <- pf(Fstar, df1, df2, lower.tail = FALSE)

  data.frame(grand, SSTR, SSE, MSTR, MSE, Fstar, pval)
}

out <- anova_summary(
  n = c(6, 6, 6),
  xbar = c(1.33, 2.50, 2.67),
  s2 = c(1.87, 2.30, 1.47)
)

round(out, 3)
```
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.notebox style="font-size: 0.58em; line-height: 1.10; padding: 8px 11px; margin-bottom: 6px;"}
<span class="label">Campus café example</span>
:::

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
anova_summary <- function(n, xbar, s2) {
  k <- length(n)
  N <- sum(n)

  grand <- sum(n * xbar) / N
  SSTR <- sum(n * (xbar - grand)^2)
  SSE <- sum((n - 1) * s2)

  df1 <- k - 1
  df2 <- N - k

  MSTR <- SSTR / df1
  MSE <- SSE / df2
  Fstar <- MSTR / MSE
  pval <- pf(Fstar, df1, df2, lower.tail = FALSE)

  data.frame(grand, SSTR, SSE, MSTR, MSE, Fstar, pval)
}

out <- anova_summary(
  n = c(6, 6, 6),
  xbar = c(7.0, 8.5, 10.2),
  s2 = c(2.0, 2.8, 3.1)
)

round(out, 3)
```

## Example: Basketball Drill Scores

:::: {.example-grid style="display: grid; grid-template-columns: 0.88fr 1.12fr; grid-template-rows: auto auto; gap: 10px 18px; align-items: stretch;"}

::: {.taskbox style="grid-column: 1; grid-row: 1; font-size: 0.63em; line-height: 1.16; padding: 11px 15px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
A coach tests three practice formats and records shooting-drill scores.

<br>

| Classic | Streak challenge | Leaderboard |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 18 | 23 | 30 |
| 20 | 25 | 29 |
| 19 | 26 | 31 |
| 22 | 24 | 28 |
| 21 | 27 | 32 |
| 20 | 25 | 30 |

Test whether the three population mean scores are equal.
:::

::: {.stat-card style="grid-column: 2; grid-row: 1; font-size: 0.77em; line-height: 1.13; padding: 13px 17px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Manual ANOVA pieces</span>

$$
\bar x_1=20,
\qquad
\bar x_2=25,
\qquad
\bar x_3=30,
\qquad
\bar x=25
$$

$$
SSTr=6(20-25)^2+6(25-25)^2+6(30-25)^2=300
$$

$$
SSE=(5)(2)+(5)(2)+(5)(2)=30
$$

$$
MSTr=150,
\qquad
MSE=2,
\qquad
F^*=75
$$
:::

::: {.notebox style="grid-column: 1; grid-row: 2; font-size: 0.61em; line-height: 1.13; padding: 10px 14px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Decision</span>

$$F^*\sim F_{2,15}$$

The p-value is extremely small.
:::

::: {.examplebox style="grid-column: 2; grid-row: 2; font-size: 0.64em; line-height: 1.14; padding: 11px 14px; margin-bottom: 0; display: flex; align-items: center;"}
Reject $H_0$. There is strong evidence that at least one practice format has a different population mean shooting-drill score.
:::

## Assumptions of ANOVA

::: {.notebox style="font-size: 0.72em; line-height: 1.24; padding: 15px 18px; margin-top: 10px;"}
<span class="label">Assumptions</span>

<ul class="assumption-list" style="gap: 10px;">
  <li>Observations are independent.</li>
  <li>Error terms, or residuals, are Normal.</li>
  <li>All groups have the same population variance: $\sigma_1^2=\sigma_2^2=\cdots=\sigma_k^2=\sigma^2$.</li>
</ul>
:::

::: {.defbox .fragment}
The common variance is estimated using the Mean Squared Error from ANOVA:

$$
\hat\sigma^2=MSE
$$
:::

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
This is why the denominator of the F statistic is $MSE$: it estimates the shared within-group variance.
:::

---

## What If ANOVA Rejects?

:::: {.two-col-wide}
::: {.col}
::: {.defbox}
ANOVA's alternative is broad:

$$
H_a:\text{at least one mean is different}
$$

So after rejecting $H_0$, we still need to ask:

**Which mean or means are different?**
:::
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.notebox .fragment}
<span class="label">Pairwise comparisons</span>

Compare the means in pairs.

For three groups:

- $\mu_1$ vs. $\mu_2$
- $\mu_1$ vs. $\mu_3$
- $\mu_2$ vs. $\mu_3$
:::

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
Number of comparisons:

$$
\binom{k}{2}
$$
:::
:::
::::

---

## Pairwise Confidence Intervals

::: {.defbox}
For comparing two group means after ANOVA, use intervals for:

$$
\mu_i-\mu_j
$$
:::

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.stat-card .fragment}
<span class="label">Fisher's LSD</span>

$$
(\bar x_i-\bar x_j)\pm
t_{1-\alpha/2,n-k}
\sqrt{MSE\left(\frac{1}{n_i}+\frac{1}{n_j}\right)}
$$

More power, but does not control experiment-wise Type I error.
:::

::: {.stat-card .fragment}
<span class="label">Bonferroni</span>

$$
(\bar x_i-\bar x_j)\pm
t_{1-\alpha/(2m),n-k}
\sqrt{MSE\left(\frac{1}{n_i}+\frac{1}{n_j}\right)}
$$

where $m=\binom{k}{2}$. Controls experiment-wise Type I error.
:::
::::

---

## Fisher LSD vs. Bonferroni

| Method | Main idea | Tradeoff |
|---|---|---|
| Fisher LSD | Uses ordinary pairwise confidence intervals after ANOVA | Higher power, but does not control experiment-wise Type I error |
| Bonferroni | Makes each pairwise interval wider by adjusting for $m$ comparisons | Controls experiment-wise Type I error, but has lower power |

::: {.notebox .fragment}
<span class="label">Least significant difference</span>

$$
LSD=t_{1-\alpha/2,v}
\sqrt{MSE\left(\frac{1}{n_i}+\frac{1}{n_j}\right)}
$$

Conclude two means differ if:

$$
|\bar x_i-\bar x_j|>LSD
$$
:::

---

## Example: Which Basketball Drills Differ?

:::: {.example-grid style="display: grid; grid-template-columns: 0.88fr 1.12fr; grid-template-rows: auto auto; gap: 10px 18px; align-items: stretch;"}

::: {.taskbox style="grid-column: 1; grid-row: 1; font-size: 0.63em; line-height: 1.16; padding: 11px 15px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
The basketball ANOVA rejected $H_0$.

Group means:

$$
\bar x_1=20,
\qquad
\bar x_2=25,
\qquad
\bar x_3=30
$$

ANOVA gave:

$$
MSE=2,
\qquad
v=n-k=15
$$

Use pairwise confidence intervals to compare the drills.
:::

::: {.stat-card style="grid-column: 2; grid-row: 1; font-size: 0.75em; line-height: 1.10; padding: 12px 16px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Fisher LSD intervals</span>

$$
SE=\sqrt{2\left(\frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{6}\right)}=0.8165
$$

$$
t_{0.975,15}=2.131
$$

$$
LSD=2.131(0.8165)=1.74
$$

| Pair | Difference | Fisher LSD CI |
|---|---:|---:|
| Classic - Streak | -5 | $(-6.74,-3.26)$ |
| Classic - Leaderboard | -10 | $(-11.74,-8.26)$ |
| Streak - Leaderboard | -5 | $(-6.74,-3.26)$ |
:::

::: {.notebox style="grid-column: 1; grid-row: 2; font-size: 0.61em; line-height: 1.13; padding: 10px 14px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Number of comparisons</span>

There are:

$$
\binom{3}{2}=3
$$

pairwise comparisons.
:::

::: {.examplebox style="grid-column: 2; grid-row: 2; font-size: 0.64em; line-height: 1.14; padding: 11px 14px; margin-bottom: 0; display: flex; align-items: center;"}
All three Fisher LSD intervals avoid 0, so each pair of practice formats has different population mean shooting-drill scores.
:::

## Example: Phone Case Drop-Test Costs

:::: {.example-grid style="display: grid; grid-template-columns: 0.88fr 1.12fr; grid-template-rows: auto auto; gap: 10px 18px; align-items: stretch;"}

::: {.taskbox style="grid-column: 1; grid-row: 1; font-size: 0.61em; line-height: 1.13; padding: 10px 14px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
A device lab tests four phone case designs.

ANOVA rejects the equal-means hypothesis:

$$
F^*=112.06,
\qquad
p<0.001
$$

Group means:

| Case | Mean repair cost |
|---|---:|
| Slim | 87.50 |
| Rugged | 113.00 |
| Wallet | 98.50 |
| Clear | 75.88 |

$MSE=17.89$ and $v=28$.
:::

::: {.stat-card style="grid-column: 2; grid-row: 1; font-size: 0.72em; line-height: 1.10; padding: 12px 16px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Bonferroni setup</span>

There are:

$$
m=\binom{4}{2}=6
$$

comparisons.

Bonferroni uses:

$$
t_{1-\alpha/(2m),28}
=
t_{1-0.05/(12),28}
=2.839
$$

For equal sample sizes $n_i=8$:

$$
SE=\sqrt{17.89\left(\frac18+\frac18\right)}=2.115
$$

Bonferroni margin:

$$
2.839(2.115)=6.00
$$
:::

::: {.notebox style="grid-column: 1; grid-row: 2; font-size: 0.61em; line-height: 1.13; padding: 10px 14px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
<span class="label">Question</span>

Which phone case designs have different population mean repair costs?
:::

::: {.examplebox style="grid-column: 2; grid-row: 2; font-size: 0.60em; line-height: 1.10; padding: 10px 13px; margin-bottom: 0;"}
| Pair | Difference | Bonferroni CI |
|---|---:|---:|
| Slim - Rugged | -25.50 | $(-31.50,-19.50)$ |
| Slim - Wallet | -11.00 | $(-17.00,-5.00)$ |
| Slim - Clear | 11.63 | $(5.62,17.63)$ |
| Rugged - Wallet | 14.50 | $(8.50,20.50)$ |
| Rugged - Clear | 37.13 | $(31.12,43.13)$ |
| Wallet - Clear | 22.63 | $(16.62,28.63)$ |

All intervals avoid 0, so all pairs differ here.
:::

::::

## Check in R: Pairwise Comparisons {.pairwise-r-check}

<style>
.reveal section.pairwise-r-check .cm-editor,
.reveal section.pairwise-r-check .cm-content,
.reveal section.pairwise-r-check .cm-line,
.reveal section.pairwise-r-check pre,
.reveal section.pairwise-r-check code {
  font-size: 0.66em !important;
  line-height: 0.98 !important;
}

.reveal section.pairwise-r-check .cell-output,
.reveal section.pairwise-r-check .cell-output-stdout,
.reveal section.pairwise-r-check .cell-output pre {
  font-size: 0.56em !important;
  line-height: 0.96 !important;
  white-space: pre !important;
}

.reveal section.pairwise-r-check .notebox { margin-bottom: 5px !important; }
</style>

:::: {.two-col-wide style="grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr; gap: 18px; align-items: start;"}

::: {.col}
::: {.notebox style="font-size: 0.58em; line-height: 1.10; padding: 8px 11px; margin-bottom: 6px;"}
<span class="label">Basketball Fisher / Bonferroni intervals</span>
:::

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
means <- c(Classic = 20, Streak = 25, Leaderboard = 30)
n <- c(6, 6, 6)
names(n) <- names(means)

MSE <- 2
v <- 15
alpha <- 0.05
m <- choose(length(means), 2)

pairs <- combn(names(means), 2)

out <- lapply(seq_len(ncol(pairs)), function(a) {
  i <- pairs[1, a]
  j <- pairs[2, a]

  diff <- means[i] - means[j]
  se <- sqrt(MSE * (1/n[i] + 1/n[j]))

  data.frame(
    pair = paste(i, "-", j),
    diff = diff,
    LSD_low = diff - qt(1 - alpha/2, v) * se,
    LSD_up = diff + qt(1 - alpha/2, v) * se,
    Bonf_low = diff - qt(1 - alpha/(2*m), v) * se,
    Bonf_up = diff + qt(1 - alpha/(2*m), v) * se
  )
})

round(do.call(rbind, out), 2)
```
:::

::: {.col}
::: {.notebox style="font-size: 0.58em; line-height: 1.10; padding: 8px 11px; margin-bottom: 6px;"}
<span class="label">Phone case Bonferroni intervals</span>
:::

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
means <- c(Slim = 87.5, Rugged = 113.0, Wallet = 98.5, Clear = 75.875)
n <- rep(8, 4)
names(n) <- names(means)

MSE <- 17.8884
v <- 28
alpha <- 0.05
m <- choose(length(means), 2)

pairs <- combn(names(means), 2)

out <- lapply(seq_len(ncol(pairs)), function(a) {
  i <- pairs[1, a]
  j <- pairs[2, a]

  diff <- means[i] - means[j]
  se <- sqrt(MSE * (1/n[i] + 1/n[j]))

  data.frame(
    pair = paste(i, "-", j),
    diff = diff,
    bonf_low = diff - qt(1 - alpha/(2*m), v) * se,
    bonf_up = diff + qt(1 - alpha/(2*m), v) * se
  )
})

round(do.call(rbind, out), 2)
```
:::

::::

---

## Bonferroni vs. Fisher: Decision Guide

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">Use Fisher LSD when...</span>

- You want a simpler post-ANOVA comparison.
- You accept higher experiment-wise Type I error risk.
- Power is the priority.
:::

::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">Use Bonferroni when...</span>

- You want stronger control of experiment-wise Type I error.
- You have many pairwise comparisons.
- You are okay with wider intervals and lower power.
:::
::::

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
Textbook takeaway: Bonferroni corrects the multiple-comparisons problem; Fisher LSD is easier and more powerful but does not maintain the same experiment-wise error control.
:::

---

##  {.quiz-question}

:::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
## Question

A one-way ANOVA with $k=4$ groups has a significant p-value. How many pairwise mean comparisons are possible?
::::

- 3
- [6]{.correct data-explanation="The number of pairwise comparisons is choose(k, 2). With k = 4, choose(4, 2) = 6."}
- 8
- 16

---

## Final Checklist

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">Before calculating ANOVA</span>

- Identify the response variable.
- Identify the grouping variable.
- State $H_0:\mu_1=\cdots=\mu_k$.
- Check independence, Normal errors, and equal variance.
:::

::: {.card .fragment}
<span class="label">After calculating ANOVA</span>

- Fill in df, SS, MS, and $F^*$.
- Use the right-tail F p-value.
- Reject only when the p-value is small.
- If ANOVA rejects, use pairwise comparisons to find which means differ.
:::
::::

::: {.thinkbox .fragment}
**One slide takeaway.** ANOVA compares several means by asking whether between-group variation is large compared with within-group error variation.
:::
